data.title: Office Macros Permitted From Internet Sources
data.summary:
Documents originating from the internet could execute macros after a single user prompt.
Macro execution was not restricted by policy, and no distinction was made between internal
and externally sourced files.
data.description:
Macros remain effective because the control is delegated to the user at the moment they
are least able to exercise it — when the document appears to be the invoice, CV or
statement they were expecting.

Platform defaults have improved, with macros from internet-marked files blocked outright,
but the protection depends on the mark-of-the-web surviving. Files extracted from archive
formats, delivered through sync clients, or passed through tools that do not preserve the
mark arrive unmarked and are treated as local.

Where macros have a genuine internal use, the answer is signing and scoping rather than a
blanket permission, which is usually what is found in place instead.
data.recommendation:
* Block macros in files originating from the internet by policy, not by relying on the
  application default.
* Verify that the mark-of-the-web survives archive extraction and sync clients, which is
  where the control most often fails.
* Permit only signed macros for the business cases that genuinely require them, scoped to
  trusted locations.
* Remove legacy document formats where they no longer have a business purpose.
data.short_recommendation: Block internet-sourced macros by policy and verify mark-of-the-web survives.
